blocks.text:
After a tropical breakfast, an excursion to the world-famous statue of Christ the Redeemer on Corcovado. A specially designed train climbs from the foot of the mountain through the Tijuca Forest, where you may spot toucans and monkeys. At the summit, 710 metres above sea level, stands the iconic 38-metre statue, with a stunning panorama of the whole city: Guanabara Bay, Maracanã Stadium, Sugar Loaf, Copacabana, Ipanema and Gávea Mountain. Lunch at a local restaurant.

Continue to the historic centre: the Lapa Arches, an 18th-century aqueduct that once carried water from the Carioca River to the city centre; the famous Selarón Steps, covered in vibrant tiles collected from all over the world; the Municipal Theatre, inspired by the Paris Opera; and the striking Metropolitan Cathedral, which can hold up to 20,000 people.

Then visit the Samba City (Cidade do Samba), the complex of warehouses where Rio’s most famous samba schools build and store their floats and costumes. Your guide reveals the secrets of designing and building them; in the exhibition hall, discover the history of samba and Carnival through images and videos, try on an authentic Carnival costume for photos, learn basic samba steps with an expert and finish with the “flavour of samba”, a classic caipirinha. Dinner at the hotel.
Christ the Redeemer statue and visitors on Corcovado in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil

blocks.text: Sugar Loaf and the hillside communities

After breakfast, head to Sugar Loaf. A magnificent cable car takes you first to Urca Hill, halfway between the ground and the summit, where you can enjoy a cocktail or taste Brazilian specialities. From the top, Rio unfolds from a new perspective: Copacabana stretching to the horizon, with the outlines of the Two Brothers and Gávea mountains, the small Red Beach (Praia Vermelha) below, and to your right Guanabara Bay, the Rio–Niterói Bridge, Botafogo and the centre, beneath the silhouette of Christ the Redeemer. Lunch at a local restaurant.

Next, a guided visit to one of the favelas of the city’s southern zone. The word “favela” comes from a plant of the hills of Bahia: in 1897, soldiers returning from the Canudos War settled on the Morro da Providência in the city centre and named it after the hill where they had camped. Today Rio has several hundred favelas, home to families, workers and small businesses, with lively streets, markets and handicrafts, and an integral part of the city’s social and cultural fabric. Walk through the streets, visit local shops and bars, and hear an honest account of everyday life in the community. Dinner at the hotel.
